title: Completion tracking vs competency verification
description: Completion tracking shows someone finished training; competency verification shows they can do the work to standard. How they differ and when each is enough.
shortAnswer: Completion tracking records that a person finished a training activity, usually with a date and sometimes a quiz score. Competency verification is a judgment, based on valid, sufficient, authentic, and current evidence, that a person can perform a task to a defined standard. Completion shows exposure to training; verification shows capability. Regulated, high risk tasks usually need verification, while low risk awareness topics may only need completion.
keyTakeaways: A completion record proves attendance or exposure, not the ability to perform.
Competency verification uses defined standards and evidence, often including observation in a realiztic setting.
Rules of evidence from vocational training (validity, sufficiency, authenticity, currency) are a useful model for workplace verification.
Even e-learning standards distinguish the two: cmi5 separates completed from passed.
Most organizations need both, matched to risk.

sections.heading: What is the core difference between completion tracking and competency verification?

blocks.text: The core difference is what the record proves: a completion shows that training was delivered and finished, while a verification shows that the person was assessed against a standard and judged capable. The first is an activity record; the second is an evidence based judgment.

The distinction is built into modern e-learning standards. The cmi5 specification treats "completed" and "passed" as separate verbs, and lets course designers choose whether a unit is satisfied by completion, by passing against a mastery score, or by both ([cmi5 specification](https://github.com/AICC/CMI-5_Spec_Current/blob/quartz/cmi5_spec.md)). See [xAPI vs cmi5](/compare/xapi-vs-cmi5). Even a pass, however, only shows success in the assessment that was designed; it is only as good as that assessment.

[Verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) goes further, typically combining knowledge checks with observed performance of the real task, judged by a qualified assessor against defined criteria.

blocks.text: Competency evidence is credible when it meets explicit rules of evidence. Vocational training regulation offers models. In United States Registered Apprenticeship, competency-based programs must identify "an appropriate means of testing and evaluation" for each competency ([29 CFR 29.5(b)(2)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-A/part-29/section-29.5)). Vocational regulators can go further and define what good evidence looks like: the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA), for example, sets these out for Registered Training Organisations under Standard 1.4 of the 2025 Standards, and they are a sound model for workplace verification too ([ASQA](https://www.asqa.gov.au/for-providers/standards-for-RTOs/practice-guides/quality-area-1-training-and-assessment/assessment-practice-guide)).

blocks.text: ASQA's principles of assessment add that valid assessment "includes practical application components that enable the VET student to demonstrate the relevant skills and knowledge in a practical setting". A completion record alone cannot meet that test.

Completion tracking is enough when the goal is awareness and the consequences of misunderstanding are low; competency verification is needed when an error could cause harm, breach a legal obligation, or when a regulator expects evidence of capability. The choice should follow risk, not convenience.

In the United States, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) goes further for forklift operators: training must include "evaluation of the operator's performance in the workplace", and the employer must ensure each operator "is competent to operate a powered industrial truck safely" ([29 CFR 1910.178(l)](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.178)).

Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act requires special education before a worker is assigned designated dangerous or harmful work ([details](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training)). For high risk work, it is hard to show training was adequate without some check that people can apply it. See [how to set up verification of competency](/guides/how-to-set-up-verification-of-competency).

sections.heading: How do completion tracking and verification work together?

blocks.text: They work together as stages: completion tracking confirms that people received the knowledge component, and verification confirms they can apply it. A risk tiered model keeps the cost of verification proportionate.

items: Classify each training requirement by consequence of error (for example low, medium, high).
Medium: completion plus a scored knowledge or scenario assessment with a pass mark.
High: completion, scored assessment, and observed verification by a qualified assessor, repeated on a set cycle.
Record all stages against the same content version so the evidence chain is complete for audit ([how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit)).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines assessment points in the knowledge framework before content is written, so each important concept or task has a stated way of being checked. Organizations can then choose where completion is sufficient and where verification, including hybrid human verification, is required.

faqs.q: Is a quiz at the end of e-learning a competency assessment?
faqs.a: It can be part of one. A well designed scenario quiz tests knowledge and judgment, but most practical competencies also need evidence of performance, such as observation. A quiz that tests recall of text on the previous screen is weak evidence of anything beyond short term memory.

Often as evidence that training was provided. For higher risk obligations, regulators and auditors may ask how the organization knows people understood and can apply the training, which completion alone does not show.

faqs.q: How often should competency be reverified?
faqs.a: It depends on risk, how often the task is performed, and how often procedures change. Many organizations set shorter cycles for high risk or infrequent tasks and reverify after incidents or procedural changes. The currency rule of evidence is the underlying principle.

faqs.q: Can technology verify competency without a human assessor?
faqs.a: Simulations and scenario assessments can provide strong evidence for some skills. For many practical and judgment based tasks, a qualified human still needs to observe and make the final judgment, which is why hybrid approaches combine automated evidence with human sign off.
